title: Gateless Barrier, Case 11: Chao-chou and the Hermits
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 11 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Zhaozhou asks two hermits "Do you have it?" and answers the same raised fist with scorn from one and a deep bow for the other. Nomon sketches Zhaozhou's long life, including his pilgrimage at age 80, and retells the story of his stone bridge that "lets horses cross," then recalls crossing a humble log bridge on a snowy hike near Mount Baker. From there Nomon questions what approval and comparison do to us, reading Wumen's verse and Seung Sahn's commentary, which quotes the Tao Te Ching on seeking the approval of others. Nomon closes by observing that whatever work we do, someone is looking to us.

Thanks for being here.

Did you enjoy doing a different service?

Do you ever think about this when you're here?
It's really weird that anybody would come and do this.
Pretty strange.

I think about that too.
Over the years, my teacher, Norman Fischer, started talking less and less about these kinds of stories.
I asked him about it once, and he said, well, they're important.
They're our family stories, and we should know them.
But actually there are probably more useful things to talk about than these whole stories.
I feel that way.
They're important, and we haven't talked about them that much, so we're going to end up spending probably over a year just getting through this set of 48 in this particular book.
I apologize for that.
I don't know how useful they are.
But maybe it's planting some seeds, and some different ways of looking at things and being in your life will pop up and be useful.
But some of it's just like being around the dinner table when Uncle Frank has got to tell the story again.
They're kind of like that, too.
They're the family stories.
So they're useful and they're not.
I think it's a bit of a mistake, in the trope of religious literature, to present stuff as perfect and true, absolutely from on high the most important thing you could ever hear.
How could anyone know that?
How could anyone know what the most important thing for you to hear would be?
But since you came to the Zen Center: Zen stories.
In the 11th koan in the Mumonkan collection, we again meet Master Zhaozhou.
You might remember him from the first case, the one about whether dogs have buddha nature.
He's the teacher who famously answered no, which in Japanese Zen got turned into the Japanese voicing of the Chinese word wu, and became the great practice of mu.
Just breathe with this sound, this idea of negation of negation, basically.
Letting go of yes or no.
Letting go of categories.
Letting go of everything.
Just mu.
And the master who put this collection together loved that koan, studied it intensively, and had important realizations from it.
I think in one of the talks I read some of his enthusiastic introduction.
You remember this, where he talks about practicing with mu being like swallowing a red-hot iron ball that you cannot spit out.
So there's an intensity to this practice.
Even though we're pretty mellow about it, we still want to honor and recognize that there's some intensity here that actually is helpful.
It's just that we would love to learn how to do that intensity in a kind way, in a gentle way, in a way that doesn't just cause more trouble for ourselves and everybody else.
We don't want to be the kind of place that's so Zen and so pure and so intense that nobody would come.
But I think we shouldn't misunderstand our relative mellowness as somehow denigrating the intense flavor and the strong practice flavor of Zen.
It's important, I think.
So these koans are very much from that tradition, the strong, strong practice.
Zhao Zhou, this teacher, is a wonderful character in these stories.
He's supposed to have lived from 778 to 897 in China.
If you do the math, that's 120 years.
And his biography, which the scholars tell us is not really a biography, probably, is what I learned in Buddhist studies to call hagiography, hagiography, just kind of an embellished biography.
So we don't really know what any of these people really did exactly.
But the traditional biography emphasizes some wonderful traits, so we can be inspired by Zhao Zhou whether there was an individual who lived 120 years or not.
What it emphasizes really is long, patient practice, and both humility and confidence.
Long practice, humility and confidence.
He did start his formal practice at 18, which doesn't seem too late, though a lot of them started earlier than that.
He's still a young man.
It just took him a really long time to mature enough to feel that he should step out of the monastery and be a teacher.
His main teacher was Nan Chuan, whom we'll meet in a few cases.
You may have heard the famous story of Nan Chuan and a cat.
We'll meet that in a couple of weeks.
And Nan Chuan, Zhao Zhou's teacher, was himself a student of the great master Matsu, or master Ma.
So these are important characters in our lineage: Zhao Zhou, Nan Chuan, Matsu.
Some of the koans are about obscure teachers that we don't know much about, but these three we do, supposedly.
Anyway, he just kept practicing.
He just kept practicing at Nan Chuan's monastery until he was 80 years old.
So those of us who are not yet 80, we've got a ways to go.
Those of us who are 80, I don't know why you're still here.
Some of us need a little longer.
It's true.
It's true.
So maybe he was a bit premature.
Anyway, he practiced until he was 80.
The stories say he kept practicing with Nan Chuan, and I looked it up.
Nan Chuan's dates are such that he was 30 years older than Zhao Zhou, and he died in 835 versus Zhao Zhou's 897.
So according to that math, his teacher died when he was 58.
So maybe he studied with somebody else for the next 22 years, I don't know.
But he stayed at the monastery of his teacher until he was 80.

One of the Zen customs, we're told, was that once you received the teacher's seal of approval and it was time to go off and teach on your own, you would go off on a pilgrimage, just on your own, maybe with one fellow monk, not a big deal, dressed humbly.
Zhao Zhou did that when he was 80.
Sometimes this pilgrimage is described as a way to test your understanding, they say, by meeting other teachers and having them check you out.
That's a kind of aggressive way of talking, to test somebody.

I think that is true, but it's maybe a little more that you go to other practice places and meet other teachers in order to enter more fully into the community of practice, into the depth and breadth of practice.

You may see and learn something with a different flavor or a different sense than what your teacher demonstrated and taught you, which is never to say your teacher was wrong, but that there's a broader vision, always a broader vision.
I did this in a small way.
When Norman Fischer asked me and Florence Caplow to ordain, whatever that was, 95 or something, 96 maybe, we were really shocked.
Our jaws hit the floor.
So I went to see several different teachers, and I think Florence did too, in different centers, some which I'd been to before, some which I'd never been to before.
I sought out teachers, just meeting with them individually or going to the retreats, to ask them, what does that mean?
What does it mean to ordain in the Zen tradition?
And I got different answers.
Exactly like I was saying, it broadened my feeling, my understanding, but didn't contradict what I learned from my teacher and would continue to learn for the next 20 years.
I wish I'd done more of that.
It's a great thing to do.
We're actually scheming to facilitate a little bit, maybe to have some sangha trips to go to other centers.
Wouldn't that be fun?
Maybe in the fall we'll start that.
But we can always learn more, right, even if we're not yet 80.

So anyway, when Giao Giao was putting on his straw sandals to begin this pilgrimage, he famously declared, "On my pilgrimage, if I meet an old man of 90 who has something to learn from me, I will teach him.
And if I meet a young girl of nine who has something to teach me, I will learn from her."
Is that nice?
"If I meet an old man of 90 who has something to learn from me, I will teach him.
If I meet a young girl of nine who has something to teach me, I'll learn from her."
And that's the same feeling for us, I think, the same feeling of confidence and humility.
But of course, in Chinese society, older people are really revered and younger people not so much.
So it's maybe even a little more radical for him to say that than for me to say that.
After a few years of pilgrimage, it's not recorded how long, he found a rundown temple below a mountain by a town.
The town was called Jiaojiao, and he took that name as his teaching name.
Before that, he had a different name, which I couldn't find out.
I'm sure it's known.
This is part of what's confusing about studying the Zen literature: these guys would change their names several times over the course of their career.
One time this came up when we were at sesshin with Norman at Loon Lake.
We decided we should call him Loon from then on.
But it didn't stick.
So I guess you should call me Red.
Anyway, it was a temple devoted to the bodhisattva of compassion.
Avalokiteshvara, whom we mentioned in the service, is the Sanskrit, and Guanyin Yuan, more or less, is the Chinese.
I just read that that temple still exists.
We can go visit it.
Maybe we will one day.
If we visit Buddhist sites in Seattle, we'll go to Hubei province, China next.
The other thing which still exists to this day is a very well constructed and elegant stone bridge in the town of Jiaojiao.
The town has a slightly different name now.
Even back then in the 9th century, this bridge was famous, and now it's the oldest standing stone bridge in all of China.
That's quite a distinction.
Huge ancient culture like that.
Jiaojiao is heavily represented in these koan collections.
He's in five of the 48 stories of the Mumonkan that we're looking at.
He's in 12 of the hundred stories in the Blue Cliff record, and he's probably in the other ones too.
And that bridge figures into my all-time favorite Zen koan, from which I take a lot of encouragement and comfort and have learned, and am still learning.
It's one of the 12 that he's in in the other collection, the Blue Cliff record.
It's about the bridge.
The story is, a monk visited Jiaojiao and asked, "I hear so much about the stone bridge, reputed to be in this territory.
But as I see it, there's no more here than an old log.
How is that?"
I've heard about the great stone bridge of Jiaojiao and all I see is this old log.
The master said, "You see the old log and you don't see the stone bridge."
"What is a stone bridge then?" the visiting monk demanded.
And the master's answer was, "It lets horses cross.
It lets asses cross."
Asses like donkeys.
The usual reading of the story is, here's another monk on pilgrimage.
Probably a little less mature, not 80.
A 30-year-old whippersnapper.
Enthusiastic, probably very well reported, and the robes just right, and so on.
We all know people like that.
He shows up, he's visiting different monasteries, and he's heard that master Jiaojiao is an important teacher, a great teacher.
And what does he find?
This rundown temple.
This somewhat funky looking old priest.
Pretty old by then.
Maybe he's 90, 100 by then.
And the place is not in the best shape either, the temple itself.
It's not too shiny.
It's well taken care of, but it's a rundown building with rundown furnishings.
Another story about Jiaojiao is that once the special ceremonial chair broke, one of the legs split.
The temple manager went to the teacher to ask for funds to go to town and hire a carpenter to fix the important chair.
And Jiaojiao said, no, no, no, no.
He went over to the fireplace and grabbed a charred piece of firewood and some string, some cord, and lashed that onto the broken leg, splinting it.
And no one dared fix the chair after that.
So he was very thrifty and his place was a little funky.
So along comes this monk, expecting to see a great Zen master, and he sees this.
He's unimpressed.
And so he says, in a pretty obvious code, I'm not impressed with you, buddy.
I came here to see the great bridge, the great bridge of Jiaojiao, and it's just this old log bridge here.
I've always loved the way the master is just unfazed.
Not insulted, doesn't whack him, none of the 30 blow stuff.
He supports the monk, he really supports the monk and encourages him to be curious by just pointing out what he sees.
Oh, you don't see the stone bridge?
You just see a log bridge?
Huh.
So that's kind of like my life ambition: somebody says something really challenging to me, to you, maybe a little insulting, and we just go to curiosity.
"Huh, isn't that interesting that you think I'm a such and so?
Huh.
I wonder why that would be.
Oh, you have reasons?
Oh, okay, tell me.
Oh, interesting."
And it did kind of wake up the monk, the visiting monk.
He asked, "Well, what is the stone bridge?
What is the stone bridge?"
And the teacher says, well, it doesn't matter how lovely the bridge is.
What matters is that we help people across, right?
It's not about being impressive.
It's about love.
So he says it lets horses cross, it lets asses cross.
So that's my plan too.
We should be log bridges for each other, don't you think?
A couple of weeks ago, Bob and Terrell and I went on a snowy adventure up to the high meadow with a little shelter in it where we go for the mountains and rivers hiking retreat.
If you haven't done that, and if it's within your body's capacity, I really recommend it.
It's wonderful.
It's like an eight mile backpack.
Such a wonderful place, this high meadow right below Mount Baker.
When Mount Baker's out, it's just like, oh, right there.
And there's beautiful alpine and subalpine vegetation.
Just lovely.
But anyway, we've been trying to get there for a couple of years in the winter when there's a lot of snow, right?
It's a different thing.
The roads are closed and so on.
So we finally tried to back route.
On the back route, you have to cross the middle fork of the Nookstack River, which is like rushing.
One time Terrell and I waded across and we barely escaped with our lives.
I didn't want to do that again.
So this time we're like, huh, will we be able to make it across?
Will we be able to get to the shelter in the winter?
It was actually April, but there was nine feet of snow, so it counts as winter, I guess.
And anyway, what were we delighted to see?
A log bridge.
A humble log bridge.
So I thought about Zhaozhou as we crossed.
Horses crossed, asses crossed, backpackers and students crossed.
So anyway, that's the back story about Zhaozhou.
Tonight's story, case 11, is called Zhaozhou's Hermits.
It goes like this.
*So then Mr.
Zhaozhou went to where a hermit was practicing and asked, "Do you have it?
Do you have it?"
And the hermit held up a fist.
And Mr.
Zhaozhou said, "You are a blind dog.
A ship cannot anchor in such shallow water."
Then he left.
Coming upon another hermit's retreat later, he asked again, "Do you have it?
Do you have it?"
Guess what the other hermit did?
Raised up a fist.
And Mr.
Zhaozhou said, "You are free to give, free to take, free to kill, and free to give life," and bow deeply.*
So then Mr.
Zhaozhou visited one hermit, asked this question, "Do you have it?"
The hermit responded non-verbally.
Zhaozhou said, "You're a blind dog.
A ship couldn't anchor in such shallow water."
And left.
Same exchange again, another time.
This time: "You are free to give, free to take, free to kill, and free to take life," and a deep, deep bow.
So apparently it's not actually clear in the Chinese whether we're talking about one hermit or two hermits.
The different translations gloss it differently because we always want to make a story that makes sense.
So it might be the same hermit, which would be even more interesting, I think.
The same hermit doing the same thing, apparently, and the teacher responding so differently.
But maybe it doesn't really matter.
Zhaozhou's response goes from what appears on the surface to be scorn the first time: like a dog, shallow.
Dogs are pretty low creatures, I understand, in Chinese culture, and I think it would mean more or less the same for us.
It sounds deprecating.
You call somebody shallow, that's not a good thing, right?
The ways we talk are so funny, though.
We're not like, "That doesn't make any sense.
Shallow?
What does that mean?
I'm not a puddle.
Deep?
What would that mean?"
But anyway, we have the same language, apparently, which makes you wonder why these things are so consistent across cultures.
But that's another question.
And the other time, what seems to be a deep statement of approval, an honoring of the monk's freedom, freedom to navigate life and death itself.
And in the second one, bowing deeply is a pretty big deal.
The Zen master doesn't bow deeply to you just because they're in the mood to mean something.
So on the surface, it seems like just a sort of puzzle that doesn't make sense.
But it's good to let these stories sit in your heart and think about them.
And think about the underlying assumptions that we always bring to every story, including the story of our life.
So here's a story about comparison.
And we're always comparing things, aren't we?
What's the difference between the two hermits, or the two visits to the same hermit as the case may be?
And are we really different in the ways that we think we are?
Are we similar in the ways that we think we are?
And a really important question here, about approval: do we all need approval from someone?
Do we need approval from authority figures, from friends, from family?
Do we need approval from ourselves?
I talk to people a fair amount, I have that honor, and I listen to my own head talking sometimes.
It seems like the one most likely to not give ourselves approval is who?
Ourselves.
So it's an interesting story about approval.
Does a teacher approve sometimes and disapprove other times?
And does that matter to the hermits?
Our first reading is like, yeah, of course it matters.
I want the A.
Does it matter in that way?
Is a life lived based on seeking approval such a good life?
Maybe it's a deep teaching on letting go of needing approval.
And the first hermit is the enlightened hermit.
Doesn't mind a bit.
"Thank you.
Great teacher.
If I'm a dad, if I'm a dog, you're a cat.
You can throw your anchor on my head anytime you want.
I'll keep practicing."
And it's interesting to think about power and hierarchy, which is implied here.
The teacher, who in this story has the name (the hermit or hermits don't have names), seems to be the one asking the questions and getting the punch line in.
Can we be our own teachers with our own questions and our own punch line?
And can we listen to our teachers in a way that really is skillful and really is helpful?
And the teacher can't really figure somebody out anyway.
Maybe it's my relative unenlightenment, but what I have noticed is when I try to figure somebody out, it pretty much always leads to trouble.
And yet my experience is that there is something that happens.
Over years and decades of practice, something changes, something shifts, something settles.
Maybe "deepens" is a good word.
I mean, it's the only word available, but "deepens" implies a kind of shallow duality.

I was thinking, if there were really such a thing as practice leads to deepening, and we could somehow measure the deepening, then we could all right now get up and get in line by order of deepness and have the shallow person at one end and the deepest person at the other end, right?
That would be perfectly logical, right?
We should probably do that routinely.
We should enter the dharma hall in the proper order.
Yeah, probably then really nobody would come back.
But what if that deepening and shallowing was in our minds and hearts and we just were pretending it wasn't, just a little below the surface?
Maybe that's even worse.

But anyway, what I noticed, though, is that even though I don't think I can figure anybody out, or at least, on a good day, I remember I can't figure anyone out, somehow in the interview room, when teacher and student meet, something really valuable can happen.
What is that?
And what happened between Jiaozhu and the hermits?
There's some connection.
There's some calling forth between these two humans in their different positions, but with their complete human hearts.
That's really powerful, really healing.
But it's more of an emergence from meeting than the teacher giving and the student receiving, or anything like that.
Or both are giving and receiving at the same time.
So maybe that's the deep point of this teaching: that Jiaozhu and the hermits were meeting in a deep way.
In this story, Jiaozhu got the speaking parts and the hermits had their fist.
But I think it would be a mistake to think that one was rejected and one was approved.

More important, I think, to study the nature of rejection, the nature of approval, the nature of meeting, and get curious about whether we can do that more fully, more intimately, and more lovingly for the healing of us all.

So Master Wu Man, who collected these stories, the guy with the red hot iron ball and the Mu thing, he wrote verses about each one, which mostly I have not been sharing with you because I don't think they're mostly that helpful, personally, but I'm not enlightened, so what do I know?
But this one I think is pretty interesting.
And just for time, I tend to run over, but in this case, let's spend a few minutes with Master Wu Man.
His verse commentary on this story is this.
*Both alike raised their fists.
Why was one accepted and another rejected?
Please tell me, what is the confusion here?
If you can utter a turning word, you will realize that Master Zhaozhou's tongue has no bone.
He helps some to get up while knocking others to the ground with perfect freedom.
However, it's important to realize that the two hermits could also see through the old master.
If you say that one hermit was better or worse, you lack the eye of realization.
If you say that neither hermit was better or worse, you still lack the eye of realization.*
It's pretty good.
Remember that the hermits could see through the teacher, so it was a two-way situation.
And in our attempts to make sense of this, we should think more deeply.
He's saying, if you think that one is better or worse, that's not right.
If you think that neither is better or worse, that's not right either.
So the whole thing is for us to be more free from comparison, and not be caught by thinking we can avoid comparison, right?
Assuming that it's all one or something like this.
So the great Korean Zen master, Sung Sun, has an interesting little short commentary on this too.
So I'm bringing in other teachers tonight.
It's a very Zen kind of commentary.
Master Sung Sun was Anita Feng's first teacher, Anita Feng, the potter who made several of our Buddhas.
So we have a connection to this teacher through her.
Sung Sun said about this story:
*In this dialogue, there are two hermits.
Both were asked the same question.
Both gave the same answer.
So why on earth would Zen master Zhao Zhou approve of one and disapprove of the other?
In our modern society, messages, images, and media are constantly telling us what to do and enticing us on what to get to improve our situation.
We hear things like, you should follow this path, or you should live your life this way, or you need to get this to make your life complete, or you aren't safe unless you buy this product.
Lao Tzu tells us in the Dao Te Ching, "If you seek for the approval of others, you become their prisoner.
How much do you believe in your true self?"
This is Dao Te Ching.
"If you seek for the approval of others, you become their prisoner.
How much do you believe in your true self?"*
*This koan is a kyung chul mun, a single entry gate koan.
Only one answer is possible.
What is the one thing?
There is only one way in this koan and not two ways.
If you enter the world of opposites, you are lost.
If you are not tangled, then you can see through old Zhao Zhou's comments.
There is one path of discovery.
You must relinquish your opinion, your condition, and your situation.
Forget about Zhao Zhou's approval or disapproval.
Ask your own true self the same question and see if you trust what appears.*
Zen master Sung Sun once said, *"Together these two monks killed Zhao Zhou and stuffed his body into a wine bottle."* Again, the Zen thing is pretty strange, to quote that with such great approval.
Of course, "kill" means to be free from or free with, and understand "to kill" means to deeply understand Zen language.
So what do you think?
What would it be if we really could change our relationship to opinions, preferences, approval, expectations?

What if somebody asked you a question and you were in complete confidence that your answer was just good enough, and you could really just be yourself and listen and learn and walk on stone bridges and log bridges, be shallow, be deep, and help people across, to practice for all beings, whether that's as hermits or school teachers or nurses or historians or retired people who help out here all the time, or whatever we're doing?
Because whatever you do, someone is looking to you.
What do they see?
How do you respond?
So that's my take on case 11, Zhaozhou and the hermits.
Thank you for listening to these talks so patiently, and one day we'll talk about something else.
